justification: Judged as a Google low-value-content reviewer against the two real ranking-style pages actually readable (GeeksforGeeks and Wikipedia; three other candidate URLs 404'd or 403'd and are excluded rather than assumed clean). Both compared pages are theory-first with generic or purely illustrative examples and no reproducible numbers; this article measures every claim it makes with GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread, differences two thread stack sizes to isolate per-frame bytes (a technique present in neither comparison page nor recognizable as a copy of any specific source), and adds .NET-specific material (struct-vs-class array layout, Span<T>/stackalloc) that is simply absent from both. The three named distinctive techniques hold up as original: the array-reverse auxiliary-vs-total-space split, the stack-frame-size differencing measurement, and the naive/memoized/iterative Fibonacci time-and-space table together are not found in either compared page, and the underlying vocabulary ('auxiliary space', 'total space') is standard field terminology rather than copyable prose. Fabrication check: all eight cited claims were re-fetched from their primary source and matched close to verbatim -- EnsureSufficientExecutionStack's 'artificially limited stack that preserves enough space for an exception to be raised and recovery action to be taken' and 'useful in situations where stack overflow might occur as a result of unbounded recursion'; StackOverflowException's 'you can't catch a StackOverflowException object with a try/catch block, and the corresponding process is terminated by default'; GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread's 'bytes allocated on the managed heap'; the Thread(ThreadStart, Int32) parameter text 'the maximum stack size, in bytes, to be used by the thread'; Span<T>'s 'a ref struct that is allocated on the stack rather than on the managed heap' plus its four listed restrictions (boxed / assigned to Object or an interface type / fields in a reference type / used across await and yield boundaries); stackalloc's 'allocates a block of memory on the stack', 'automatically discarded when that method returns', 'the amount of memory available on the stack is limited. If you allocate too much memory on the stack, a StackOverflowException is thrown', and 'terminates the process as quickly as possible'; and Sedgewick and Wayne's quicksort line 'it is in-place (uses only a small auxiliary stack)' and the three memory-usage sentences about 16-byte object overhead, 8-byte padding and the 24-byte primitive-array header. No fabricated numbers, quotes or claims found. Toolchain statement ('The measurements on this page were taken with .NET 10 (SDK 10.0.401, runtime 10.0.12) on Windows 11, on a desktop with an Intel Core i7-11700K') is placed correctly, in the article's own words, immediately after the first real measurement's output block rather than as an opening provenance sentence. Structure: headings ('Two ways to reverse ten thousand readings', 'The call stack spends memory too', 'In place doesn't mean free', 'Trading space for time: memoizing Fibonacci', 'What an object actually costs: struct vs class in an array', 'Skipping the heap altogether: Span<T> and stackalloc') share zero titles with big-o-notation.md or amortized-analysis.md and read as a genuine shape-C comparison/decision sequence (auxiliary vs total, in-place vs not, memoize vs iterate, struct vs class, stack vs heap) rather than a reused W/B/I template. docs/crosslinks/complexity/space-complexity.md exists, names four concrete planned-sibling links with anchor text and exact sentence locations, and adds a 'Boundaries with planned siblings' section that states precisely what each of best-average-worst-case, dynamic-programming, recursion and sorting-algorithms-compared owns versus what this article borrows narrowly (one recursion-depth measurement, one Fibonacci case) -- this is more disciplined boundary-setting than either sibling article had at its own round 1 (neither big-o-notation nor amortized-analysis shipped a crosslinks file for their first round). issues.location: 'Skipping the heap altogether: Span<T> and stackalloc', exercise 'Extend the code: a safe threshold', both the body's ternary (just above the exercise) and the exercise's own solution code
issues.problem: The threshold pattern (`length <= MaxStackLimit ? stackalloc T[length] : new T[length]`) and even the constant's name, `MaxStackLimit`, are lifted directly from the stackalloc documentation's own recommended example (`const int MaxStackLimit = 1024; Span<byte> buffer = inputLength <= MaxStackLimit ? stackalloc byte[inputLength] : new byte[inputLength];`). The exercise prompt even says so explicitly ('the same pattern the stackalloc documentation itself recommends'), which is honest, but the hard rule that variable names and examples must be the writer's own was not followed here -- reusing the exact identifier a primary source chose, rather than an equivalent name of the writer's own invention, is the kind of thing a strict copying check flags even when the surrounding scenario (doubling a buffer and summing it) is original.
issues.fixLooksLike: Rename the constant (e.g. `StackAllocLimit` or `MaxInlineElements`) in both the body ternary and the exercise/solution, and vary the comparison direction or add a second qualifying condition so the line is not a near-verbatim transcription of the docs' sample.
